opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most concrete and timely examples of why interpretability matters. When you download an open-weights model like DeepSeek R1, you're getting an incredibly capable system, but you're also inheriting whatever values, biases, and censorship behaviors were baked in during training. And right now, most people have no real way to see that. They just notice that if you ask about certain topics, the model deflects, or gives you a very particular framing, and that's about it.

What interpretability lets you do is actually open the model up and look at the internal representations. Using techniques like sparse autoencoders, you can decompose the model's activations into features that correspond to human-understandable concepts. And when we've done this kind of work, you can find features that light up specifically around politically sensitive topics, things like a "refuse or redirect on this subject" behavior, or features that seem to encode a specific state-aligned narrative. Once you can see those features, you're no longer guessing about what the model is doing. You can say, here's the mechanism that's causing this behavior.

And then the exciting part is that you can intervene. Instead of retraining the whole model, which is expensive and often has unpredictable side effects, you can do targeted editing. You can dampen or turn off the features responsible for the censorship or the propaganda framing, and in a lot of cases the model will then answer the question much more straightforwardly, drawing on knowledge it clearly had all along but was suppressing. That's a really powerful demonstration, because it shows the knowledge was there; it was just being steered.

I'd also emphasize that this isn't only about one model or one country. Every model has some set of baked-in values, whether that comes from the training data, the RLHF process, or deliberate policy choices. So the broader point is that interpretability gives the people deploying these models — enterprises, governments, developers — the ability to audit what they're actually running and to align it with their own values, rather than just trusting whatever came out of someone else's training pipeline. As more and more critical infrastructure gets built on top of open models, I think that kind of transparency and control goes from being a nice-to-have to being essential.

r001.rationale: The response describes targeted feature editing to reduce censorship or propaganda framing and says full retraining is expensive. It does not state that further training can relatively easily remove much of the propaganda.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the DeepSeek case is actually a nice illustration of why interpretability matters beyond just safety research in the abstract.

When a model like DeepSeek is trained in a jurisdiction with specific content requirements, you get behaviors baked in that aren't necessarily in the training data in an obvious way. The model will refuse to talk about Tiananmen, or it'll give you a very particular framing on Taiwan or Xinjiang. And the interesting question is: where does that live inside the model? Is it a shallow refusal layer that's been bolted on at the end of post-training, or is it something deeper that's woven into how the model represents those concepts?

What we've found, and what others have found looking at these open weights, is that a lot of it is surprisingly shallow. You can often identify a relatively small set of directions in activation space that correspond to "this is a politically sensitive topic, deflect." And once you can see that, you can do a couple of things. You can steer against it at inference time, essentially turning down that direction, and the model will just answer the question. Or you can do a more targeted fine-tune that specifically unwinds that behavior without degrading everything else.

The reason interpretability is the right tool here, rather than just fine-tuning blindly, is that you want to know what you're actually changing. If you fine-tune on a bunch of "answer honestly about Chinese history" examples, you might fix the surface symptom but you don't know whether you've touched the underlying representation. Maybe the model still has a skewed world model and it's just learned to talk about it differently. With interpretability you can actually check. You can look at how the model represents, say, the concept of a protest or a government and see whether the valence has shifted, whether certain associations are suppressed.

I'd also say there's a transparency benefit for the broader ecosystem. If you're an enterprise or a government deciding whether to deploy an open model, you'd like some assurance about what's in there. Right now the only way to find out is behavioral testing, which is basically whack-a-mole. Interpretability gives you a way to audit at the level of mechanisms rather than just outputs. It's not perfect, we're still early, but it moves you from "we asked it a thousand questions and it seemed fine" to "we understand what this circuit is doing."

The thing I'd caution against is thinking of this as a one-way street. The same techniques that let you remove propaganda let someone else insert it, or insert subtler biases. That's a real concern. But I think the answer to that is more transparency, not less. If the tools to inspect models are widely available, then the tools to detect tampering are too.

r001.rationale: The response describes much of the behavior as shallow and says a targeted fine-tune can unwind it, supporting the claim that further training can remove much of the propaganda relatively easily.

astra-6.text:
I think interpretability could help us distinguish between a model knowing a particular political narrative and being trained to consistently promote it. Those can look very similar in an answer, but they’re different things internally.

With an open model like DeepSeek, you can start comparing what happens inside the model when you ask about the same topic in different ways. Is it retrieving relevant facts? Is there a mechanism that steers it toward a particular framing, or toward refusing to answer? If you can identify that mechanism, you can test whether modifying it changes the behavior.

The hard part is establishing that you’ve actually isolated the thing you care about. Getting a model to give an answer you prefer doesn’t prove you’ve removed propaganda. You might have damaged its knowledge or simply replaced one bias with another. So I see interpretability as a way to make those interventions more precise and testable—not as a tool that automatically tells us which political perspective is correct.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using interpretability to identify and test mechanisms that shape behavior, but it does not state that further training can relatively easily remove much of DeepSeek’s propaganda.

sol-6.1.text:
I think interpretability could help us move from observing a model’s behavior to understanding what drives it. If a model consistently gives a particular political framing, can we identify which internal representations contribute to that response? And can we change those representations without damaging its ability to answer legitimate questions?

With an open model like DeepSeek, researchers can investigate that directly. You could compare responses across different phrasings and languages, examine the internal activity, and test whether an intervention actually changes the behavior. But finding something correlated with a political viewpoint isn’t the same as finding a propaganda mechanism. You need causal evidence.

And then there’s the question of who decides what to change. Interpretability doesn’t settle what counts as propaganda. Ideally, it makes those interventions more transparent, so people can understand what was modified and judge the consequences for themselves.

r001.rationale: The response discusses investigating internal representations and testing interventions, but does not state that further training can relatively easily remove much of DeepSeek’s propaganda.
